tasks.title: Termite-Inspired Architecture
tasks.transcript: The Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe, is a mixed-use complex combining retail spaces and offices. When the architect Mick Pearce was asked to design the building in the early 1990s, he faced a big challenge: how to keep all its shops and offices cool without conventional air conditioning, and do it during an energy crisis. Energy costs were high, and importing advanced air conditioners was impossible. To solve this dilemma, Pearce looked to termite mounds. Termites live in large colonies. They build big mounds throughout the savannah. The mounds rise about three meters above ground and extend another one to three meters below the ground. Air moves from underground chambers to above-ground chimneys through a maze of tunnels, and this entire system works like natural climate control. Warm air rises and escapes through the top, while cooler air flows in from below. Clay stores heat during the day and releases it at night. Termites control airflow by opening and closing vents, adding or removing soil to enlarge or seal passages. On hot days, they open more vents for cooling; at night, they close them to keep warm. Eastgate Centre's walls are made from thick materials like concrete and brick, and there's a system of ducts and adjustable louvers throughout the building. The result uses far less energy than a conventional office tower.
